question: What first drew you to dance, and when did you know you wanted to pursue it seriously?
lookingFor: A genuine personal origin story tied to a real turning point, not a generic 'I've always loved dance'.

bullets: Name a specific memory or moment, not a vague love of dance
Explain what shifted it from hobby to serious commitment
Connect it to why they're applying now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started dancing at six because my older cousin dragged me to her class, but the moment it became serious was watching a touring contemporary company do a piece about migration when I was fourteen. I remember thinking movement could say things words couldn't, and I went home and tried to make my own short piece about it that same week. From then on I stopped seeing it as an after-school activity and started building my week around training. That's the pull that's brought me here.

commonMistakes: A vague 'I've always loved to dance' with no real moment
Describing dance purely as exercise or a hobby with no depth
Skipping straight to achievements instead of the actual origin
followUps: What did your family think when you decided to pursue it seriously?

question: Talk us through your dance training so far. What styles have you studied and where?
lookingFor: A clear, organized account of formal and informal training that shows range and depth, not just a list.

bullets: Name the main styles or schools studied with rough duration
Mention any formal exams, grades, or notable teachers
Reflect on what each style actually gave them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I trained in classical ballet through the Royal Academy of Dance syllabus up to grade six, and alongside that I've done contemporary and jazz at a local studio for about five years. Ballet gave me the discipline and placement that everything else sits on top of, while contemporary is where I actually found my own voice as a mover. More recently I've been taking workshops in West African dance, which has completely changed how I think about rhythm and weight. Each style has taught me something the others couldn't.

commonMistakes: Reciting a list of studios and years with no reflection
Only mentioning one style with no sense of range
Exaggerating grades or achievements that don't hold up under a follow-up
followUps: Which of those styles do you feel least confident in, and why?

question: Why pursue a dance degree rather than going straight into a company or conservatoire-style training?
lookingFor: Understanding of what a degree adds beyond technique class, not a defensive 'backup plan' framing.

bullets: Show understanding that a degree offers more than technique training
Be genuine, not defensive, about wanting breadth
Connect it to a personal goal like choreographing, teaching, or writing about dance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I love performing, but what pulled me toward a degree rather than straight conservatoire training is that I want to understand dance as well as do it, its history, the theory behind composition, how it sits next to other art forms. I've already choreographed a couple of short pieces for my school and realized I want proper grounding in that side, not just more technique class. A degree also keeps the door open to teaching or arts administration later, which matters to me. I don't see it as a step back from performing, I see it as building a wider set of tools.

commonMistakes: Implying the degree is a fallback if performing doesn't work out
No real answer beyond 'I want a degree to be safe'
Dismissing the academic side as unimportant
followUps: What academic subject within dance are you most looking forward to studying?

question: Why do you want to study dance here specifically, rather than at another institution?
lookingFor: Specific, researched knowledge of the program's faculty, repertoire, or approach, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific faculty member, module, or performance opportunity
Connect it to their own interests or gaps in their training
Show they compared it to alternatives, not just applied everywhere
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked at a few programs, but yours is one of the only ones that lets students choreograph for the main stage in second year rather than waiting until final year, and that early practical responsibility is exactly what I want. I also read about your visiting artist scheme, and the residency with a physical theatre company last year is close to the kind of interdisciplinary work I want to make. Most other courses I looked at were far more performance-only, and I wanted somewhere that treats making work as seriously as performing it.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that could apply to any dance program
Naming the wrong faculty member or an outdated detail
Focusing only on reputation or rankings
followUps: What would you want to contribute to the department beyond your own performing?

question: Is there a choreographer or company whose work you particularly admire? What draws you to them?
lookingFor: Specific, informed engagement with a real body of work, not just a name-drop.

bullets: Name a specific choreographer or company and a specific piece
Explain what about their approach or aesthetic resonates
Ideally connect it to the applicant's own work or thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep coming back to Crystal Pite's work, especially Betroffenheit, because of how she uses a whole ensemble to physicalize something as internal as grief and trauma. What draws me in is the way the movement never feels decorative, every gesture seems to be doing narrative work. I tried something similar on a much smaller scale in a duet I made about anxiety, using unison and breaking it to show two people falling in and out of sync. Watching her work made me braver about using stillness.

commonMistakes: Naming a famous choreographer with no specific piece or detail
Confusing the choreographer's work with someone else's
No connection back to their own practice or interests
followUps: What's something about their work you'd push back on or do differently?

question: Tell us about a performance, live or recorded, that changed the way you think about dance.
lookingFor: A specific, reflective response showing genuine engagement, not just naming a famous show.

bullets: Name a specific piece and describe what actually happened in it
Explain the shift in thinking, not just that they enjoyed it
Connect it to their own practice or values
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I saw a small company perform a piece made entirely without music, just breath and footfall, and it completely reset what I thought dance needed to work. Before that I assumed rhythm had to come from a score, but watching them build tension purely from silence and timing showed me rhythm is something the body generates itself. I went back and reworked a solo I'd been struggling with by stripping the music out entirely, and it was a much stronger piece for it. It's the performance that taught me to trust movement on its own terms.

commonMistakes: Describing the performance without saying how their thinking changed
Picking something they clearly haven't watched closely
Staying at the level of 'it was beautiful' with no substance
followUps: Have you tried applying that idea again since, and how did it go?

question: Have you ever dealt with an injury or physical setback that affected your training? How did you handle it?
lookingFor: Honest account of a real setback showing maturity, patience, and what they learned about their own body.

bullets: Describe the injury or setback honestly, without minimizing it
Explain what they actually did during recovery, not just 'rested'
Reflect on a lasting change to how they train now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I tore a ligament in my ankle during a jump combination in my second year of training and was out of full classes for nearly four months. It was frustrating watching from the side, but I used the time to sit in on rehearsals taking notes on choreography and started strength work for my feet that I'd never bothered with before. When I came back I was actually a more careful, more aware dancer, I stopped rushing through warm-up. It taught me that my body is something I have to manage long-term, not just push through.

commonMistakes: Downplaying the injury to seem tough
No real detail on how the recovery time was actually used
No lasting change in behavior or perspective afterward
followUps: How do you approach injury prevention now?

question: Dance degrees ask you to be both a rigorous performer and a critical thinker writing essays about the field. How do you feel about that balance?
lookingFor: Realistic understanding that a degree isn't pure studio time, and genuine respect for the academic side.

bullets: Show awareness that critical writing is a real, substantial part of the course
Explain why understanding dance's history or theory matters to their own practice
Give a concrete example of already engaging with both sides
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I actually looked forward to that mix when I was choosing courses, because I've noticed my own choreography gets better when I understand the context I'm working in. For a school project I wrote about how postmodern choreographers rejected narrative and virtuosity, and using some of those ideas directly changed a piece I was making at the time. I know the writing side will be hard, especially citing sources properly and defending an argument, but I'd rather be pushed on that than only ever train in the studio. The two feed each other for me.

commonMistakes: Treating the academic side as an obstacle to get through
Claiming to love essay writing with no evidence they've done any
Not connecting the two sides at all
followUps: What's a piece of dance writing or theory you've found genuinely difficult, and why?

question: What's the difference between choreography and improvisation, and how do they relate to each other?
lookingFor: Clear conceptual grasp of the distinction and awareness that they're not opposites but often work together.

bullets: Define choreography as set, structured, repeatable movement
Define improvisation as spontaneous, in-the-moment movement generation
Explain how improvisation is often used to generate material that later becomes choreography
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Choreography is movement that's been set and structured so it can be repeated the same way each time, while improvisation is movement generated in the moment, responding to music, a prompt, or another dancer without a fixed plan. They're not really opposites though, a lot of choreography actually starts life as improvisation, where a choreographer generates raw material by improvising and then selects and refines what works into a set structure. I use improvisation a lot in my own process for exactly that reason, it gets me past the movements I'd choose consciously.

commonMistakes: Treating them as strict opposites with no overlap
Confusing improvisation with just 'freestyling badly'
Giving a definition with no real-world example
followUps: Do you personally find improvising or setting choreography harder, and why?

question: What do you understand by 'musicality' in dance?
lookingFor: Understanding that musicality is more than counting beats, it's phrasing, dynamics, and interpretation.

bullets: Go beyond 'staying on the beat' to phrasing and dynamics
Mention responding to accents, silences, and texture, not just tempo
Give a concrete example from their own dancing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Musicality is more than hitting the counts, it's about how you phrase movement in relation to everything happening in the music, the accents, the silences, the texture underneath the main melody. Two dancers can do the exact same steps on the exact same counts and look completely different because one is only tracking the beat and the other is responding to the whole piece. For me it clicked when a teacher had us dance to a piece with no clear beat at all, and I realized musicality is really about listening, not counting.

commonMistakes: Defining musicality as simply staying on the beat
No concrete example to back up the definition
Assuming musicality only applies to dances set to music with a clear rhythm
followUps: How would your musicality change dancing to silence versus a driving rhythm?

question: How would you explain the key differences between classical ballet and contemporary dance to someone who knows nothing about either?
lookingFor: A clear, non-jargon explanation covering technique and philosophy, not just 'one is old and one is new'.

bullets: Contrast ballet's turned-out, codified vocabulary with contemporary's use of the floor, weight, and release
Mention differing relationships to narrative and to the audience
Avoid implying one style is superior to the other
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Ballet works from a codified vocabulary, turnout, pointed feet, very specific positions of the arms and legs, that's been passed down and refined for centuries, and it tends to value lightness and lift. Contemporary dance grew partly as a reaction against that, it uses the floor, weight, and gravity much more, and it doesn't have one fixed vocabulary, different choreographers develop their own movement language. Neither is easier, ballet demands incredible precision and contemporary demands you build your own technique often from scratch, and honestly training in both has made me a better dancer in each.

commonMistakes: Implying contemporary dance has 'no technique' or 'no rules'
Framing one style as more advanced or serious than the other
Explaining costume or shoes instead of the actual movement principles
followUps: Which do you find more physically demanding, and why?

question: Are you familiar with any frameworks for analyzing or describing movement, like Laban Movement Analysis? What do you find useful about them?
lookingFor: Some genuine familiarity with a movement-analysis framework and an honest sense of its practical use, not textbook recitation.

bullets: Name a framework, most likely Laban, and roughly what it categorizes, such as effort qualities of weight, time, space, and flow
Explain a practical use, like giving vocabulary for describing movement quality in rehearsal
Be honest about the depth of familiarity rather than overclaiming expertise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've studied the basics of Laban Movement Analysis, particularly the effort qualities, weight, time, space, and flow, and I found it useful because it gives you a vocabulary for describing quality of movement, not just shape. Before that, when a teacher told me a phrase needed to feel 'more urgent,' I didn't always know what to change, but thinking in terms of quick time and direct space gave me something concrete to adjust. I'm not deeply trained in it, I've mostly picked it up through workshops and reading, but it's changed how precisely I can talk about movement with other dancers.

commonMistakes: Claiming deep expertise they don't actually have
Reciting definitions with no sense of practical use
Freezing and having nothing at all to offer on the question
followUps: Can you describe one of your own recent movement choices using that vocabulary?

question: What have you read or watched recently that's deepened your understanding of dance as a field, beyond your own training?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine intellectual curiosity and wider reading, with specific detail rather than a vague list.

bullets: Name a specific book, article, documentary, or critic and what it actually argued
Explain how it changed or challenged their thinking
Avoid a name-drop with no substance behind it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Alastair Macaulay's writing on ballet for a while, and one review of a Balanchine revival made me think differently about how much a critic's job is really about noticing what the choreography is quietly arguing, not just describing steps. I also watched a documentary on Alvin Ailey that got into how he built a company explicitly to create opportunity for Black dancers who were shut out of mainstream ballet companies at the time. It made me think more about dance institutions as political spaces, not just artistic ones, which I hadn't really considered before.

commonMistakes: Naming a source with no detail on what it actually said
Only mentioning performance videos with no critical or written engagement
Claiming to have read something they clearly haven't
followUps: Did you disagree with anything in what you read or watched?

question: How does dance relate to other art forms you're interested in, like music, visual art, or theatre?
lookingFor: Genuine interdisciplinary thinking connected to real experience, not a vague claim that all art is connected.

bullets: Name a specific other art form and a concrete connection or collaboration they've experienced
Explain what dance can do that the other form can't, or vice versa
Show curiosity about combining forms rather than treating dance in isolation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm quite drawn to the relationship between dance and visual art, I once made a piece responding directly to a series of paintings, trying to translate brushstroke and color into weight and dynamics rather than just illustrating the images. What that taught me is dance can hold ambiguity the way a painting does, it doesn't have to explain itself the way theatre often does with text. I'd love to do more work like that here, maybe collaborating with visual art or design students on a joint project.

commonMistakes: A vague 'all art is connected' with no concrete example
Only listing art forms they like with no actual link to dance
Overstating a collaboration that never really happened
followUps: What's a project you'd want to try collaborating on across disciplines?

question: Dance can be used for far more than performance, therapy, education, community work. Have you had any experience with those sides of the field, or thoughts on them?
lookingFor: Awareness that dance has applications beyond the stage, ideally backed by real experience.

bullets: Mention any hands-on experience teaching, volunteering, or assisting outside performance contexts
Show understanding of why movement can help in therapeutic or community settings
Be specific rather than making a generic claim that dance 'heals people'
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I volunteer teaching a beginners' contemporary class at a community center on Saturdays, mostly adults who never trained as kids, and it's completely changed how I think about dance's purpose. Watching someone who's nervous about their body slowly get more confident moving has nothing to do with technique or performance quality, it's about permission to take up space. I haven't studied dance movement therapy formally, but that experience has made me curious about it as a possible direction alongside performing.

commonMistakes: A vague, unearned claim that dance 'heals' or 'saves' people
No actual experience with teaching or community settings
Dismissing this side of the field as less serious than performance
followUps: What was the hardest part of teaching adults who'd never danced before?

question: What would you do if a choreographer asked you to perform a movement you fundamentally disagreed with or found physically uncomfortable?
lookingFor: Mature judgment distinguishing artistic discomfort worth pushing through from genuine physical risk, raised respectfully.

bullets: Distinguish creative discomfort, which is often part of growth, from genuine physical pain or injury risk
Describe communicating honestly and specifically rather than silently complying or refusing outright
Show respect for the choreographer's authority while still advocating for themselves
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It depends what kind of discomfort it is. If it's just outside my comfort zone artistically, something that feels emotionally exposing or technically new, I'd push through it, that's usually where growth happens and I'd trust the choreographer's vision. But if it's actually causing pain or feels like it risks injury, I'd say so immediately and specifically, not just complain vaguely, and ask if there's an alternative that achieves the same effect. I did have to do that once with a lift that was hurting my lower back, and being direct about it early meant we found a safer version without losing the moment in the piece.

commonMistakes: Saying they'd just do whatever they're told with no self-advocacy
Refusing outright with no distinction between discomfort and injury risk
Vague complaining instead of specific, constructive communication
followUps: How would you raise it if the choreographer brushed off your concern?

question: How do you typically respond to critical feedback in the studio, and can you give an example?
lookingFor: Evidence they can take feedback without defensiveness and actually apply it, shown through a concrete example.

bullets: Describe a specific piece of feedback, not a vague generalization
Show they didn't get defensive and explain the concrete change they made
Reflect on the outcome or what they learned about receiving critique
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A teacher once told me my solo looked technically clean but emotionally flat, which stung because I'd worked so hard on the technique. Instead of arguing I asked her to be specific about where it dropped, and she pointed out I was marking the transitions instead of committing to them. I went back and ran the phrase over and over just focusing on full commitment through the in-between moments, and the difference was obvious even to me. Now I try to ask 'where specifically' whenever I get feedback that feels general, it makes it actually usable.

commonMistakes: Claiming they always take feedback perfectly with no honest struggle
A vague example with no specific change made afterward
Getting defensive in the retelling of the story itself
followUps: Has feedback ever felt wrong to you? How did you handle that?

question: Beyond technical skill, what do you think separates a good dancer from a truly compelling one?
lookingFor: Thoughtful reflection on artistry, presence, or interpretation, not just a restatement of technical proficiency.

bullets: Name a quality beyond technique, such as commitment, presence, or interpretive honesty
Support it with a specific example of a dancer or performance where they saw this
Avoid dismissing technique's importance while making the point
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Technique gets you in the room, but what makes someone compelling to watch is usually commitment, dancing like they actually mean it rather than executing steps correctly. I saw a dancer once do a fairly simple phrase, nothing technically flashy, but she committed so fully to every transition that I couldn't look away, whereas more technically impressive dancers on the same bill felt safer and less alive. I try to remind myself of that in my own training, that perfect placement without full commitment reads as empty.

commonMistakes: Just restating technical proficiency as the answer
No concrete example to illustrate the point
Dismissing technique entirely as unimportant
followUps: Do you think that quality can be taught, or is it more innate?

question: Walk us through how you've gone about choreographing a piece of your own, from initial idea to finished work.
lookingFor: A genuine, specific account of a creative process, showing they've actually made work, not just performed others' choreography.

bullets: Describe where the initial idea or prompt came from
Explain a concrete step in their process, like generating material through improvisation, structuring, or editing
Reflect honestly on what worked or what they'd change
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I made a trio last year that started from a single image, three people trying to occupy the same small square of floor without touching. I generated most of the movement through improvisation tasks with the two other dancers, recording everything on my phone and then picking out the moments that felt most honest rather than the ones that looked most impressive. Structuring it was the hardest part, I kept adding too much, and it wasn't until I cut nearly a third of the material that the piece actually breathed. If I made it again I'd trust silence more, I filled almost every second with sound the first time.

commonMistakes: Describing only performing, not actually making choreography
A process with no specifics, just 'I made up some steps'
No honest reflection on what they'd change
followUps: How did you choose the music, or decide not to use any?

subtopic: A cultural or traditional dance form
question: Is there a cultural or traditional dance form that's shaped how you move or think about dance?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific engagement with a dance tradition and honest reflection on its influence, avoiding surface-level treatment.

bullets: Name a specific form and where or how they learned it
Explain a concrete way it's shaped their technique or artistic thinking, not just 'it's beautiful'
Show respect for the tradition's own context rather than treating it purely as a resource for their own work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I grew up doing Bharatanatyam alongside my contemporary training, and it's shaped how I think about storytelling through gesture far more than anything else I've studied. The mudras taught me that a single precise hand shape can carry as much meaning as a full-body phrase, and I bring that instinct for economy into contemporary work now. I'm careful about how I use it though, I try not to just borrow shapes out of context, and I want to keep studying it properly rather than letting it fade into a vague influence.

commonMistakes: Treating the tradition purely as an aesthetic resource with no context or respect
A vague 'it's beautiful' with no concrete influence described
Claiming deep expertise in a form they've only briefly encountered
followUps: How do you keep that practice going now that you're focused on other styles?

question: Can you explain what 'turnout' is in dance and where it actually comes from in the body?
lookingFor: Correct basic anatomical understanding, showing they've been taught technique safely, not just told to force their feet apart.

bullets: Define turnout as outward rotation of the leg from the hip joint
Note it should come from the hip rotators, not be forced from the knees or feet
Mention why understanding this matters for injury prevention
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Turnout is the outward rotation of the legs, and it's meant to come from the hip joint, specifically the deep external rotator muscles, not from twisting the knees or feet. A lot of dancers get injured because they force turnout by rolling in through the ankles or forcing the knees past what the hips actually allow, which puts huge strain on the joints. My teachers were strict about only turning out as far as our hips genuinely permit, and building strength in those rotator muscles rather than faking the range, and I'm glad they were, because I've seen classmates get knee injuries from forcing it.

commonMistakes: Saying turnout comes from the feet or knees rather than the hips
No mention of injury risk from forcing it
A definition with no sense of why it matters in training
followUps: How do you personally work on improving your turnout safely?

question: If I played you thirty seconds of a piece of music right now and asked you to describe how you'd start choreographing to it, what would you do?
lookingFor: Ability to think aloud about a creative process under pressure, showing genuine process rather than a rehearsed answer.

bullets: Describe listening for structural features first, like tempo, dynamics, or instrumentation, before jumping to steps
Mention using improvisation to generate initial material rather than planning everything in the head
Show comfort with uncertainty and thinking aloud rather than freezing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: First I'd just listen a few times without moving at all, trying to notice the structure, is there a clear build, does it repeat, are there silences or sudden shifts in dynamic. Then I'd probably improvise to it a few times, just seeing what my body wants to do instinctively before I plan anything consciously, and record it so I don't lose the good moments. I'd be looking for one image or feeling the music suggests to me and trying to build the phrase around that rather than trying to illustrate every note. It's a bit uncomfortable thinking about it out loud like this, but that not-knowing is honestly close to how I actually start most pieces.

commonMistakes: Freezing or refusing to engage with the hypothetical
Jumping straight to specific steps with no listening or structural thinking
Giving an overly polished, clearly rehearsed answer that doesn't sound like real thinking
followUps: What if the music had no clear beat at all, how would that change your approach?

question: What's a dance performance you've seen recently, live or on film, and what did you think of it?
lookingFor: Evidence of actively watching current dance work, with a real critical opinion rather than pure praise.

bullets: Name a specific, recent, real performance or film
Give both something they admired and something they'd critique or question
Show they engaged with it as more than passive entertainment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I saw a touring production a few months ago that reworked a folk tale through contemporary movement, and I loved how the ensemble work built tension, the way dancers kept almost-but-not-quite touching created this constant unease that fit the story. I wasn't as convinced by the lighting design though, it felt like it was trying to do the emotional work the choreography had already done, which made some sections feel a bit over-explained. It's made me think a lot about restraint, about trusting movement to carry meaning without every other element underlining it too.

commonMistakes: Only offering praise with no critical opinion at all
Naming something they clearly haven't actually watched recently
A summary of the plot with no reflection on the choreography itself
followUps: Would you have made any different choices as the choreographer?

question: How do you think technology, motion capture, dance on film, social media, is changing dance as an art form?
lookingFor: A considered, specific view rather than vague enthusiasm or dismissal, ideally grounded in something they've seen or tried.

bullets: Name a specific way technology intersects with dance, such as film, motion capture, or social media
Give a balanced view, noting both opportunities and something lost or changed
Connect it to their own experience or opinion, not just abstract commentary
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Social media has completely changed how younger dancers discover styles, I learned a lot of West African dance basics initially from short clips before I ever took a real class, and that access is genuinely valuable. But I do think it's shifted what counts as impressive, favoring tricks that read well in fifteen seconds over the slower, quieter qualities that only really land live. I got to try motion capture once at a school workshop, seeing my movement translated onto a digital figure, and it made me think about how much of dance's meaning comes from breath and effort that the technology just doesn't capture yet. I'm excited by it, but I don't think it replaces being in a room with a live body.

commonMistakes: Pure enthusiasm or pure dismissal with no nuance
No personal experience or example grounding the opinion
Treating the question as only about social media, ignoring film or motion capture
followUps: Do you think dance made specifically for film or a screen is a different art form from live dance?

subtopic: Performing through nerves or a mistake
question: Tell us about a time something went wrong during a performance. How did you handle it in the moment?
lookingFor: Composure and problem-solving under pressure, and honest reflection rather than a story where nothing actually went wrong.

bullets: Describe a real, specific mistake or mishap during a performance
Explain the concrete in-the-moment response, staying in character, adjusting, recovering
Reflect on what it taught them about performing more generally
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: During a group piece my counting slipped and I came into a formation change a full eight counts early, completely out of sync with everyone else. My instinct was to freeze, but I forced myself to keep moving with full commitment and used the extra counts to add a small transitional phrase that actually looked intentional, then found my way back into unison at the next clear marker. Nobody in the audience seemed to notice, but I noticed, and it taught me that performing confidently through a mistake matters more than the mistake itself. Now I actually rehearse for that, deliberately practicing recovery so I'm not thrown if it happens again.

commonMistakes: Claiming nothing has ever gone wrong on stage
Describing freezing or stopping with no recovery
No reflection on what it taught them going forward
followUps: How do you manage nerves before a performance in general?
